Working with Binary Objects

1. Why use Binary Objects in Key-Value API?
  • Server nodes don't need the application's Java class definitions on their classpath;
  • You can read individual fields without deserializing the entire object — faster for server-side processing;
  • Enables schema evolution — add/remove fields without breaking existing nodes;
2. Switching to Binary View
  • Use withKeepBinary() to get a binary view of any cache: 
    IgniteCache<Integer, BinaryObject> binaryCache =
    ignite.cache("PersonCache").withKeepBinary();

BinaryObject person = binaryCache.get(1);
String name = person.field("name");
int age = person.field("age");
  • The original cache still works with deserialized objects; withKeepBinary() returns a view, not a new cache;
3. Creating Binary Objects Dynamically
  • Build objects without having Java classes: 
    BinaryObject person = ignite.binary().builder("Person")
    .setField("name", "Alice")
    .setField("age", 30)
    .setField("email", "alice@example.com")
    .build();

binaryCache.put(1, person);
4. Modifying Binary Objects
  • Binary objects are immutable; create a builder from an existing object to modify: 
    BinaryObject existing = binaryCache.get(1);

BinaryObject updated = existing.toBuilder()
    .setField("age", 31)
    .setField("phone", "+1234567890")  // add new field
    .removeField("email")              // remove existing field
    .build();

binaryCache.put(1, updated);
5. Binary Objects in Entry Processors
  • Combine withKeepBinary() and entry processors for efficient server-side operations: 
    binaryCache.invoke(1, (entry, args) -> {
    BinaryObject val = entry.getValue();
    int currentAge = val.field("age");

    BinaryObject updated = val.toBuilder()
        .setField("age", currentAge + 1)
        .build();

    entry.setValue(updated);
    return null;
});
  • This reads and updates a field without ever deserializing the full object;
